newsitem.title: UK: UK MPs worried LDC debt reduction plan faltering.
newsitem.headline: UK MPs worried LDC debt reduction plan faltering.

text.p: UK Parliament's Treasury Committee expressed concern on Wednesday that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is dragging its feet over an innovative scheme to reduce the debt burdens of the world's poorest countries.

In particular, the members of parliament urged the IMF to implement a decision in principle to sell part of its gold reserves to finance debt relief -- an idea long backed by British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

"We are concerned that the initial impetus of the Chancellor's initiative, which has been sustained for two years, could soon begin to wane and believe that as, according to the Chancellor, The decision has in effect been taken that gold sales will take place if necessary', the Fund must now act.
"Debt relief for the poorest heavily indebted countries must not be allowed to founder," the committee, drawn from members of parliament from all three main parties, said.

The IMF and other multilateral financial institutions must now contribute in a substantial manner to the debt reduction process, especially as they are owed about a fifth of the total debt of the poorest 20 heavily indebted nations, it added.
The IMF's executive board was due to discuss later on Wednesday whether to launch the multilateral debt reduction initiative by providing Uganda with up to $385 million of relief.

But the committee said it was perplexed that, five months after the scheme was agreed at the IMF annual meeting in Washington, there appeared to be no definitive list of countries that could expect to benefit from it.
"We fear an excessive degree of prevarication, particularly by the board of the Fund," the MPs concluded.

They said Clarke should require Britain's executive director at the IMF to seek as soon as possible a definitive list of beneficiaries and the proposed timescale over which the initiative would bear fruit.

The MPs also recommended that Clarke should press the Fund's board to establish an independent evaluation unit with a wide remit to cover, in particular, the impact of IMF structural adjustment programmes on the economies of sub-Saharan Africa.
They were prompted to make the proposal after being unable to make their minds up whether such programmes were useful.
"The committee was presented with such conflicting information that it has been impossible to disentangle the evidence sufficiently to arrive at any, even tentative, conclusions," the MPs said.

The panel also proposed that the chancellor of the exchequer provide it with an annual report on the work of Britain's executive director and the activities of the Fund and that a hearing be held on the report at least every two years.
